title_en: Canceled Mass Effect Universe Would Have Finally Answered Your Trilogy Ending Questions, Writer Says
summary_en: BioWare's canceled Mass Effect Universe would have addressed Mass Effect 3's controversial endings and the fates of Shepard's squadmates.
body_en:
BioWare's canceled Mass Effect Universe would have addressed Mass Effect 3's controversial endings and the fates of Shepard's squadmates, one of the game's writers has said.
For more than a decade, Mass Effect fans have debated how BioWare could reconcile the wildly divergent endings of Mass Effect 3 — and satisfy players who insisted that their particular ending choice should be canon (I see you, Destroy fans). But according to one of the writers behind the now-canceled Mass Effect Universe, the studio had actually cracked the puzzle before EA scrapped the project and closed BioWare forever.
Speaking during a reddit fan Q&A supporting the "Save Mass Effect" fan movement, Mass Effect: Annihilation novel author Cat Valente — who spent three years on the writing team for the unfinished sequel — offered a bittersweet glimpse into how the narrative team approached the franchise's biggest lingering questions.
While strict NDAs signed with published EA continue to prevent Valente from revealing specific plot details, she emphasized that reconciling Mass Effect 3's endings was front and center for the game's writers room, and noted that the team wasn't relying on a single silver bullet to bridge the 600-year narrative gap between the original trilogy and this upcoming fifth installment.
"[We] worked specifically, and for a very long and laborious time, on handling the endings in a way that wouldn't piss everyone off, at least not piss them off completely, that wouldn't make them feel like nothing mattered, wouldn't privilege any one kind of player over another, but also allow us, somehow, to actually write a coherent story going forward, within the limits of having to do it in a playable mainstream video game and not a post-modern 3000 page novel," Valente wrote.
"Not for nothing, guys, but that's *kind of a tall f***ing order*. Part of the reason it took so long and Andromeda was in Andromeda is that figuring out an elegant solution to that problem turns out to be *really hard.* An elegant solution that we can do with current game tech, that will be approved by higher-ups, that doesn't take over the whole game and make actually telling a story impossible... it takes a long time, and it's not obvious how best to pull it off when you're the people who bear responsibility for pulling off one of, if not the, hardest nut to crack in game writing.
"And it's become really clear that it's impossible to make the gaming community completely happy with anything no matter how hard you try, especially the ME endings that were so controversial, yet people feel so strongly about their own choices. We burned out so many valuable neurons going up against that problem. I know so many people think it's easy, just make Destroy canon and move on, but consider that, for example, I feel as strongly about Synthesis as others do about Destroy. And everyone feels strongly about choices mattering. Do you really think there is a single solution that would have satisfied everyone? In a *video game*?
"But we did our best, and I think we landed in a good place," she concluded. "There wasn't one single solution, but several working together, and unfortunately I can't say any more than that."
As a hugely knowledgeable fan of the original trilogy — enough that she got the gig writing Andromeda's quarian ark prequel novel — Valente emphasized that the fates of the trilogy's loyal squadmates had also been a key consideration for the Mass Effect Universe team.
"You would have been able to know everything you wanted to know about them," she said, when asked for her own thoughts of what characters such as Garrus, Tali and Wrex did next. "I don't have headcanons about those fates, I have canon-canons. I know you'd have been able to find out about them because one of my jobs was to write all those fates and their possible variations (all then submitted to the room, workshopped with everyone, and sent to higher-ups for approval...)
"God, it was like being asked to stitch a nice border on the Shroud of Turin," she continued. "I put on my Big Writer Pants for that one and gave it every bit of talent I have, because I love those characters beyond measure, and they more than earned my best."
Of course, we know that Universe would have seen at least one fan-favorite character return: Liara, now 600 years older — around middle age for a long-lived asari. But what about others? Asked for specifics, Valente noted her NDA blocked her from confirming specific names, but that there had been widespread discussion of bringing back every character possible.
"I think the best way to answer your question is to say that any character who physically *could* survive, we considered allowing to survive into the new game and made decisions on them," Valente teased. "We thought about all the things you'd have wanted us to think about, and I hope you do believe that, because it's the truth. Everyone in that room loved those characters, or loved to hate them, as much as any fan. We took each and every one of them and their fates very seriously."
So, who could have survived? Alongside the asari, the krogan are another long-lived Mass Effect species — and some fans believe we already got a glimpse at an older Grunt in the krogan civil war artwork released by BioWare a couple of years ago. Could Wrex also still be around? While he'd be ancient, it would not be impossible. Synthetic characters like EDI could certainly be around (and even if you'd picked Destroy, could surely have been rebooted eventually from a backup).
And then there are the characters and plotlines from Andromeda — a game that's nowhere near as beloved as the original Mass Effect trilogy, but whose storyline was still expected to factor into Universe in some way. Indeed, Valente revealed, Andromeda fans would have finally gained the answer to some of the spinoffs lingering questions (which were originally set to be answered in long-scrapped Andromeda sequels). For example, fans would have finally learned the identity of The Benefactor, who funded the Milky Way galaxy's push to Andromeda for unclear reasons.
"There is an answer, and it was fucking rad," Valente said. "As the author of an Andromeda tie-in, I and one of the other writers [...] worked closely on closing out Andromeda mysteries and bringing it together with the rest of the story. We know who [The Benefactor] was. At least the six of us in the writers' room know, plus anyone who approved our narratives or saw our work in-progress. I wish I could tell you, sorry."
Finally, and least surprisingly, Valente confirmed that Universe would have featured new aliens alongside the returning characters/races from the four games so far. (Would the bird-like raloi finally have appeared on-screen? We will now never know.)
"I don't think there's a problem with saying of course there were going to be new aliens?" Valente concluded. "We all pitched new species and some were accepted and moved along to art etc and some weren't. Same with the squad. All of us pitched squad members and our directors chose between the pitches. I can't give you any more than that."
While EA has officially canceled Mass Effect Universe and BioWare's offices have now closed their doors, fans are trying their best to show there's still huge interest in the franchise — even if any sort of U-turn on EA's decision currently seems unlikely. Some fans have suggested EA could alternatively be convinced to sell the Mass Effect IP to another publisher who would do something with it, but again this seems a remote possibility. EA can simply hold onto the franchise rights to leverage it in other games (N7 skins in Battlefield, anyone?) and continue profiting from ongoing merchandise and licensing revenue.
It remains a heartbreaking end for Mass Effect, though there is of course one glimmer of hope remaining: the not-yet-canceled Mass Effect TV series that remains in development for Prime Video. Should this ever escape development hell and make it to release and be a success and convince EA it should give Mass Effect another go... well, maybe we'd find out what Grunt was doing 600 years later after all.
Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social
